papers.title: SHAPE: Discrete Supervision and Parallel Continuous Streams for Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Human Data
papers.title_zh: SHAPE：从第一视角人类数据学习灵巧操作的离散监督与并行连续流
papers.abstract: Egocentric human recordings are far cheaper than dexterous robot demonstrations, promising stronger pretraining and direct skill learning without task-specific robot data. Yet humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics, so human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies, providing only retargeted end-effector (EEF) actions. This raises two questions: how human data should supervise the policy, and how a dexterous robot should read out actions at deployment. We address both in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), a vision-language-action (VLA) model whose backbone predicts discrete action tokens of EEF chunks as an auxiliary task, while a shared flow-matching expert outputs two executable streams, EEF and joint. On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, a matched study shows that discrete supervision helps learn from human data, driving backbone gradients and shaping action-informative representations across domains. Under standard control pipelines at deployment, direct joint readout excels at fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, scoring 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for π0.5, whereas IK-based EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE learns new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.

Conclusion
We presented
SHAPE
, a dexterous VLA that pairs auxiliary discrete action supervision on the backbone with a shared dual-stream action expert outputting executable EEF and joint streams. In a matched 2
$\times$
2 study, predicting discrete EEF tokens helps the policy learn from egocentric human data: it drives sustained action gradients on the backbone without dynamic reweighting or conflict with flow matching, and shapes action-informative representations while preserving last-layer task alignment across domains better than continuous regression controls. Sharing the backbone and expert transfers human pretraining to the joint stream without human joint labels, while keeping both streams executable serves complementary deployment pipelines: direct joint readout excels with robot demonstrations, whereas wrist-frame EEF readout via IK enables transfer from human demonstrations alone. Future work will explore scaling this paradigm to larger human video corpora and more robot embodiments.

Method
Problem setup
We learn a policy that maps an observation
$o_{t}$
and an instruction
$\ell$
to an action chunk
$A_{t}=[a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}]$
with
$H=64$
, from two data sources. Robot teleoperation
$\mathcal{D}_{r}$
provides head and wrist camera images, proprioception, and actions in both EEF and joint space. Egocentric human recordings
$\mathcal{D}_{h}$
provide head-camera images and tracked 3D hand poses, but lack executable joint states and actuator commands; we retarget the tracked hands to derive EEF actions.
Action parameterization.
Both action spaces are relative to the current state. For each hand, let
$T_{t}\in\mathrm{SE}(3)$
be the wrist pose at time
$t$
and
$p_{t}$
the positions of the five fingertips in the wrist frame, and let
$q_{t}$
be the joint positions. For
$k=0,\ldots,H-1$
, the EEF action contains the wrist pose expressed in the current wrist frame,
$T_{t}^{-1}T_{t+k}$
, and the fingertip offsets
$p_{t+k}-p_{t}$
; the joint action is the offset
$q_{t+k}-q_{t}$
. In pretraining, each data source is normalized with its own statistics. For human recordings, the hand is first estimated with the MANO hand model
Romero et al. (2017)
and then retargeted to the robot hand, and the fingertip positions are those of the retargeted hand. Expressing EEF actions in the current wrist frame cancels camera extrinsics and decouples the action target from the underlying arm joint configuration.

papers.title: PhysVAM: Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
papers.abstract: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution. Effective action generation therefore requires not only modeling object dynamics but also anticipating how future interactions will shape task progress. To this end, we propose \textbf{PhysVAM}, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model that represents anticipated interactions through their effects on future task progress. This value-based formulation provides task-directed foresight without reconstructing future visual states. Conditioned on current observations and historical object and robot motion, PhysVAM jointly learns action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch learns horizon-specific latent representations through future task-value prediction from successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that facilitate task success. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior task success, with absolute success-rate improvements of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines in simulation and real-world tasks, respectively. Project page: https://metarobo.github.io/physvam.github.io/.

papers.tldr: 针对动态操作中物体持续运动、预测未来状态未必揭示任务进展的问题，本文提出 PhysVAM，一种物理导向的未来价值动作模型，用交互对任务进展的影响来表征预期交互，从而在不重建未来视觉状态的前提下提供任务导向的前瞻。基于当前观测与历史信息条件化生成动作，论文展示了该方法在动态物体操作任务中的有效性，为学习型机器人操作技能提供了以价值为核心的新范式。

papers.title: Alignment Drives Reuse: Learning Generalizable Robot-Use Agents from Heterogeneous Experience
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) demonstrate broad generalization across tasks and domains. However, comparable generalization in robot manipulation remains challenging. Heterogeneity in robot embodiments, task formulations, geometric conventions, and action interfaces fragments interaction experience across benchmarks and hardware. We rethink robot skill learning through alignment: Can heterogeneous interactions across benchmarks and embodiments jointly improve one shared skillset for robot manipulation? We propose UniCraft, a framework for learning robot manipulation skills by aligning heterogeneous settings. Specifically, UniCraft represents observed scene geometry using consistent coordinate conventions and aligns sensing and control interfaces across robots. It organizes tasks from different benchmarks in a canonical format, allowing interaction feedback to jointly refine shared skills and the orchestration policy that guides their selection and composition, without any demonstrations or model weight updates. We interleave tasks from 3 benchmarks and 6 embodiments, collecting 2,700 learning rollouts per agent model. During training, UniCraft improves pooled task success on unseen scenarios and tasks by 9-28 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO, 10.8-13.3 on RoboTwin 2.0, and 3.1-14.4 on RoboCasa365 (Epochs 1-3). At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo the same gravity-aligned temporal aggregation and rasterization onto a fixed angular grid. Conclusion
We presented a LiDAR perception pipeline for end-to-end locomotion that aligns sensing and representation between simulation and reality. The proposed spherical range image provides a structured LiDAR observation that supports learning challenging locomotion skills, while scan-pattern replay, self-occlusion modeling, and shared encoding reduce perceptual discrepancies across domains. Experiments show stronger hardware transfer than other baselines, and ablations identify scan-pattern replay as the most influential component, with LiDAR-specific domain randomization and self-occlusion modeling providing additional gains.

In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.

Abstract
Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with
PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and
robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.

Conceptually, multiple peaks in the critic value landscape support diverse grasping modes, while dense, smooth guidance supports closed-loop control and recovery. PPO jointly learns the critic and policy.

Introduction
What is the essence of human’s ability to manipulate objects? How can we make robots exhibit human-level intelligence in their object manipulation performance? This remains an unsolved and even poorly understood problem
[
1
,
17
]
. Humans can grasp the same object in many different ways, adapting their wrist pose and finger configuration to the current situation
[
7
]
. This flexibility suggests a desirable capability for robotic grasping: a single policy should support multiple effective grasping modes and select suitable actions from the current hand–object state. Diversity and feedback are complementary
[
18
,
4
]
. Alternative grasping modes provide options when an approach is unfavorable, while closed-loop control allows the robot to adjust its actions and retry after failed contact
[
15
]
. The challenge is to learn a policy that retains this repertoire while realizing its behaviors through continuous physical interaction.
A useful perspective on this challenge comes from the distinction
between evaluating candidate solutions and generating them
[
8
,
2
]
.
Generative modeling offers an expressive means of representing
multiple plausible solutions, as illustrated by advances in image
and video generation
[
12
,
13
]
.
In dexterous grasping, grasp-synthesis approaches have similarly explored
large-scale grasp data and diverse grasp-pose distributions.
However, a grasp proposal alone does not specify how to reach, maintain, or recover it through physical interaction.
Conversely, some policy-learning approaches integrate grasping more
directly with feedback close-loop control, either through reinforcement
learning or subsequent policy distillation.
Yet optimizing task success does not necessarily encourage a
policy to preserve multiple successful grasping modes:
learning can concentrate on a narrow repertoire of effective
behaviors
[
6
,
11
]
.
Despite progress along both directions, jointly learning diverse
grasping strategies and reliable close-loop execution remains
a central challenge.
We revisit this challenge from a value-function perspective.
Rather than explicitly generating a target grasp pose, we seek to
learn a state-value landscape—a
scalar field over grasping states—with two key properties:
multiple high-value peaks and dense, informative guidance.
Each peak should correspond to a distinct effective grasp
configuration, allowing the landscape to represent multiple
valid ways of grasping the same object.
Far from the object, the value should generally increase as the
hand approaches a feasible grasp from different directions;
near contact, it should distinguish effective wrist poses and
finger configurations according to the object’s geometry.
I

Conclusion
We presented Dr. Grasp-RL, which uses diverse resets and a
time-reversed curriculum to train a dexterous grasping policy with PPO.
The policy acquires multiple grasping modes without a generative
architecture and combines this diversity with closed-loop control
for real-time adjustment and recovery.
Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate strong
generalization across object geometries and robust execution.
Implications.
These findings motivate a control-centered view of robot learning.
Research paradigms and narratives borrowed from other domains
may not be the best fit for the distinctive demands of robotics.
We therefore advocate developing models and architectures grounded
in robotics’ own requirements for physical interaction.

papers.title: A Sequential Quadratic Programming Perspective on Optimal Control
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between the iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator (iLQR), Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP), and Newton's method for optimal control problems. Using a unified Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) framework, we introduce Newton-LQR, a Riccati-based algorithm that solves for the exact Newton step the optimal control problem. Within this framework, we establish that iLQR is a principled modified SQP method rather than merely an approximation of DDP. We show that iLQR generates a descent direction, whereas the inclusion of dynamics Hessians in DDP and Newton-LQR may lead to indefinite quadratic subproblems and necessitate regularization. We further distinguish DDP and the proposed Newton-LQR algorithm through their treatment of costate information and second-order dynamics terms. Numerical experiments across six benchmark problems demonstrate that iLQR often exhibits superior convergence during the initial optimization phase, while Newton-LQR and DDP can exploit second-order information to accelerate convergence near a solution.

papers.tldr: 迭代LQR、微分动态规划与牛顿法在最优控制中的关系长期缺乏统一的理论刻画。作者以序列二次规划框架统一三者，提出基于Riccati递推的Newton-LQR算法求解精确牛顿步，并证明iLQR是一种有原则的修正SQP方法而非DDP的简单近似，且能产生下降方向。研究进一步指出DDP与Newton-LQR因引入动力学Hessian可能产生不定二次子问题而需要正则化，为最优控制算法设计提供了清晰的理论边界。

papers.title: RoboHarness-RL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for VLM-Based Robot Manipulation
papers.title_zh: RoboHarness-RL：基于VLM的机器人操作的智能体强化学习
papers.abstract: Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. We present RoboHarness-RL, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models. To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop LiteHarness, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance. With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%). Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to $4\times$, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/RoboHarness-RL/

RoboHarness-RL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for VLM-Based Robot Manipulation
Liyang Li
*
Mingyu Liu
*
Xiaoman LiZhiyue ZhaoJin-Chuan ShiCanyu ZhaoHaokai ZhangJinyuan TianLinhao Zhong
Hao Chen
Chunhua ShenZhejiang University, State Key Lab of CAD & CG
Abstract
Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging.
We present
RoboHarness-RL
, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls.
Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models.
To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop
LiteHarness
, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance.
With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%).
Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to
$4\times$
, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback.

Introduction
Agentic harnesses let vision-language models (VLMs) manipulate robots through tool calls for perception, planning, and control

Robot systems have traditionally separated a slow model that reasons about the task (System 2) from a fast learned policy that produces motor actions (System 1).
In a harness, this boundary blurs: the VLM not only decides what to do next, but also specifies end-effector poses and gripper commands, so its decisions directly shape how the robot moves.
Yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging.
On randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, the ORA harness reaches 69.2% success with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash but only 6.8% with the open-weight Qwen3.5-9B (Sec.
4.3
).
Approaches to improving compact VLM agents include refining the harness

,

or distilling frontier models through supervised learning
[
28
,
6
]
.
Building on these advances, we investigate whether reinforcement learning from the model’s own interactions can further improve manipulation performance beyond supervised imitation.

Where is RoboHarness-RL? It optimizes robot tool calls, which are higher-level than the motor commands of VLAs and finer-grained than the text actions of LLM agents.

In parallel, agentic RL trains language models through multi-turn tool use in digital environments such as web search
[

and graphical interfaces
[

.
Harness-based manipulation lies between the two (Fig.
2
): the VLM uses high-level tool calls as in agentic RL, while controlling physical robot actions.
Concurrent approaches include RL with a learned VLA executor
[
35
]
and single-turn RL for control-program generation
[

.
We instead train the VLM to specify robot actions itself through multi-turn tool calls.
Two challenges make RL costly in this setting.
First, every model call carries a growing interaction history, including camera images, across episodes of up to 200 calls, increasing the cost of both rollout collection and policy updates.
Second, tasks that the current policy consistently solves or fails may provide little group-relative learning signal, yet still consume rollout budget.
We address both with
RoboHarness-RL
, an agentic RL framework that trains VLMs to manipulate through tool calls, with no VLA or WAM generating actions.
After fine-tuning on teacher demonstrations, the VLM learns through multi-turn GRPO with task-outcome rewards.

Conclusion
RoboHarness-RL trains VLMs for tool-based manipulation through agentic RL, with LiteHarness supporting efficient multi-turn interaction.
RL improves success beyond teacher imitation without VLAs or WAMs, reduces repetitive calls, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback.
Gains extend to randomized scenes unseen during training.
Randomized bimanual manipulation and long-horizon tasks remain challenging; transfer to real robots remains to be evaluated.
LLM Usage Statement
Our system uses Qwen3.5-9B as the policy and GPT-6 Astra for teacher demonstrations.
The authors used ChatGPT and Claude to edit the paper and improve code, verified all content, numbers, and claims, and take full responsibility for the paper.

Limitations
Simulation.
All experiments are conducted in simulation.
Agentic RL collects many multi-call rollouts in every round, which simulation provides at scale but would be difficult to collect on real robots; evaluating transfer to real robots is left to future work.
Dependence on the teacher.
We initialize RL from teacher demonstrations because the base model rarely succeeds on its own: the untrained Qwen3.5-9B reaches 20.0% on clean RoboTwin and 1.8% on LIBERO-Pro, which leaves too few successful rollouts for RL to learn from.
RL therefore inherits the coverage of the demonstrations to some extent.
Remaining failure modes.
RL improves how the policy uses the tools, while perception, grasp proposals, and motion planning come from fixed external models.
Most remaining LIBERO-Pro failures place the object near, but not at, the required pose (Appendix
E.3
), and long-horizon tasks and randomized bimanual scenes show the largest remaining gaps (Secs.
4.2
and
4.3
).
Statistical scope.
Each RL run of 25 rounds takes about 415 GPU hours (Table
A9
), and evaluating one checkpoint takes 250 or 800 multi-call episodes.
We therefore train one RL run per benchmark and evaluate each reported checkpoint once; the paired tests in Appendix
A.6
capture variation across episodes, not across training seeds.

papers.title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
papers.title_zh: 面向智能体编排机器人操作的边界感知策略学习
papers.abstract: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.

Introduction
Robot manipulation needs both task-level decisions and precise physical interaction with objects. Agents built on general-purpose multimodal models now handle the task level through tool calls: they capture images, segment objects, plan multi-step tasks and recover when a step fails

[

,

,

agent-orchestrated robot manipulation
.
However, a policy completes its command reliably only from a limited range of states, and the agent may hand over outside this range. We refer to this range as the
handoff boundary
of the policy. These systems call an off-the-shelf policy that is trained to complete whole tasks from initial states, which leaves this boundary narrow and hard to describe in the middle of a task (
Fig.
1
a). As a result, the agent tends to hand over the whole task from the initial pose. When the policy fails, the agent corrects the arm and hands over once more, but often from a state outside the boundary, so the policy fails again, as we observe in

,

Conclusion
We presented Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which enables more reliable agent–policy coordination in agent-orchestrated robot manipulation. Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy only on contact segments with diverse start poses, so that a short handoff protocol can describe its wide and explicit handoff boundary to the agent. Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement then retrains the policy on the system’s own curated rollouts, so that the boundary extends to earlier stages of each task. With boundary-explicit training alone, the system outperforms the strongest baseline by more than 26 percentage points in randomized scenes of RoboTwin 2.0 and on RoboDojo, and self-improvement further reduces the API cost and time per episode by 41.3% and 37.5% on average without loss in success rate. These results suggest that an orchestrated system improves most when the boundary between the agent and the policy is made explicit and expanded over time.
Limitations and future work
First
, data curation discards the suboptimal segments of each rollout, which DAgger
[
31
]
or offline reinforcement learning
[
23
]
may turn into training data on how the system recovers from mistakes.
Second
, the handoff protocol describes the boundary only by rules, and a policy that outputs a confidence for the current state, like SayCan
[
1
]
, may let the agent check

papers.title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
papers.title_zh: ReFocus：长时程机器人操作强化学习的进度引导自适应练习
papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $π_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $π_{0.5}$. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.

Introduction
In long-horizon manipulation, the success of a subtask depends on both its execution and the state inherited from preceding stages. Completing one subtask therefore does not guarantee successful continuation. Imitation learning gives vision-language-action (VLA) policies a strong initialization by supervising actions along expert trajectories
[

,

,
34
]
. At deployment, however, successive subtasks begin from states produced by the policy itself, and demonstrations provide limited supervision for handling the deviations that accumulate along the way, resulting in failure.

Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables VLA policies to learn beyond demonstrations with further environmental interactions by themselves. However, most online RL methods, which learn from full-task rollouts using only binary terminal feedback, still struggle with long-horizon tasks. As illustrated in Fig.

1) Reward Imbalance.
To characterize intermediate progress, we group verifiable subtasks with shared prerequisites into stages, within which subtasks can be completed in any order. Even with prerequisite gating and one-time credit, the total reward assigned to a stage can depend on its decomposition granularity. Uniform per-subtask rewards, for example, give a stage more weight simply because it contains more completion event

Conclusion
In this work, we present ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework for long-horizon manipulation that alternates Global and Local RL to improve a shared VLA policy. Specifically, during Global RL, a DAG-based Progress Reward balances reward allocation across stages for policy training and supports bottleneck diagnosis. After identifying bottlenecks, Adaptive Practice Windows concentrate additional interaction on the corresponding bottlenecks during Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus improves the SFT baseline from 90.6% and 39.3% to 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively. A RECAP-based adaptation extends the framework to three real-world tasks, achieving 95% success on
BreadBaker
compared with 30% for the SFT-initialized
$\pi_{0.5}$
policy.

Limitations and Future Work
Some Local RL rollout modes rely on restoring intermediate simulator states. Since comparable mid-episode resets are impractical on physical hardware, the real-world experiments of ReFocus employ RECAP-based post-training on recorded rollouts as an alternative.
In current version, ReFocus employs a frontier LLM as the Scheduler, which operates between training rounds to diagnose execution bottlenecks and allocate practice windows accordingly. A direction for future work is to extend from an inter-round advisor to an online Co-Worker that remains active throughout task execution. Under this paradigm, when the VLA policy stalls at a bottleneck subtask, the Co-Worker would intervene by selecting and triggering an appropriate recovery skill, temporarily assuming control until task progress is verified, at which point execution would be returned to the policy.

However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce
ReFocus
, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates Global with Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. papers.title: Supply Geometry, Learn Execution: Screw Attention for Zero-Shot Policy Transfer in Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: We present the Screw Attention Policy, a geometry-centric manipulation framework that supplies task geometry explicitly and learns only execution. The policy operates on object poses, relative SE(3) transforms, and joint screw axes provided by perception and robot models. The policy requires only 30K learned parameters. Trained entirely in simulation on a single robot arm, the policy generalises to new scene layouts, transfers zero-shot across robot embodiments, and deploys directly on a real robot, without adaptation or fine-tuning. It achieves 96% success on LIBERO, 85.8% under layout changes, 80.2% across five unseen robot arms, and 21 of 24 trials on a real robot. These results suggest that much of what manipulation policies learn at scale is geometric structure that can instead be supplied.
papers.reason: 仿真训练的操做策略零样本迁移到真实机器人
papers.tldr: 针对操作策略泛化与仿真到真机迁移困难的问题，本文提出螺旋注意力策略，显式提供物体位姿、相对SE(3)变换与关节螺旋轴等任务几何，仅用约3万参数学习执行部分。策略完全在仿真中单机械臂训练，却能泛化到新场景布局、零样本迁移到五种未见机械臂，并直接部署到真机无需微调。实验在LIBERO达96%成功率，真机24次试验成功21次，说明几何先验可显著降低学习负担并促进跨本体迁移。

papers.title: Atomic Policy: Composing Atomic Manipulation Skills with Agentic Reasoning
papers.title_zh: Atomic Policy：用智能体推理组合原子操作技能
papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to translate task intent into physical interactions as the scene changes. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. A common phase-level interface supports specialized policies and generalist action models. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show how Atomic Policy improves task following and supports recovery in complex, long-horizon manipulation. Introduction
Long-horizon manipulation requires a robot to pursue its task goal while reasoning about a scene that changes with every interaction.
Instructions may leave intermediate steps implicit, and an unsuccessful action can alter what is feasible next.
Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a basis for this reasoning, enabling robotic agents to interpret instructions and coordinate perception, planning, and control

Perceptual and geometric tools help these agents resolve spatial relationships and ground ambiguous or underspecified instructions in the scene
[

Visual feedback then allows them to monitor progress and revise decisions as execution unfolds

Translating these decisions into reliable manipulation remains difficult.
The physical interactions available to an agent are constrained by its execution interface
[

Analytic primitives can struggle with complex grasps, constrained placement, and articulated-object interaction

We focus on how task reasoning can steer these motor behaviors while remaining responsive to their outcomes.
The agent must specify the intended interaction and its target, then determine whether the resulting state supports the next step.
Grounded steering and verification therefore become part of skill composition.
We introduce
Atomic Policy
(Fig.
1
), a framework that separates local manipulation skills from task-level reasoning and composition.
Each atomic skill is a reusable behavior with a phase-level completion condition, implemented by either a dedicated visuomotor policy or a shared language-conditioned model.
A VLM-based agentic harness estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver composes the skills according to their preconditions and effects.
The harness steers each phase through language, visual pointing, or both: language specifies the interaction and its referents, while points make spatial targets explicit.

Direct control reaches 98.0% success on Push 5 Blocks, compared with 86.3% for Atomic Policy, whereas Atomic Policy reaches 60.0% success and a score of 80.0 on Tabletop, compared with 52.0% and 69.5.
Learned skills thus matter most for contact-rich phases that require precise and timely control, while planar pushing from a static view is within reach of direct VLM control.
Future work includes automatic phase discovery and runtime selection between direct VLM control and learned skills.

Conclusion
We presented Atomic Policy, connecting symbolic planning to learned skills through a shared steering and verification interface.
Phase-specific language and 2D image points support both specialized policies and shared action models.
Experiments in 2D pushing, tabletop manipulation, and pick-and-place demonstrate the benefits of explicit steering and feedback.
Real-robot results show improved task following and illustrate recovery in complex, long-horizon tasks with ambiguous or underspecified goals.

papers.title: X-World: Transferring Video Priors to Cross-Embodiment Robot Control
papers.abstract: Language-instructed manipulation requires robust closedloop policies, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are costly and limited in coverage. Human and robot videos provide complementary spatiotemporal priors for crossembodiment control. We propose X-World, which adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views. A Q-Former compresses hidden states into tokens for a shared flowmatching expert that predicts action chunks. Datasetspecific projections map native states and actions. We adapt the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, freeze it for action-only pretraining of the Q-Former and action expert, then post-train on the target platform. At inference, X-World responds at 20 Hz and overlaps updates with execution via asynchronous real-time chunking. X-World performs strongly on LIBERO and under zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus. On hardware, it averages 81.7% success across six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e, one of three real-robot configurations presented.
papers.reason: 利用视频先验学习跨本体操作策略
papers.tldr: 语言指令操作需要鲁棒的闭环策略，但带动作标注的机器人轨迹昂贵且覆盖有限。本文提出X-World，将预训练视频扩散模型适配到多视角，用Q-Former压缩隐状态并由共享流匹配专家预测动作块，再在目标平台后训练。方法可利用人类与机器人视频先验实现跨本体控制，并以20Hz异步实时推理运行，降低了动作标注数据的依赖。

papers.title: WISER-RL: A Wake-Sleep Learning Mechanism for Robot Reinforcement Learning from One Demonstration
papers.title_zh: WISER-RL：从单次示范进行机器人强化学习的唤醒–睡眠学习机制
papers.abstract: A robot learning from one human demonstration may rarely succeed on its own, leaving reinforcement learning (RL) with little reward feedback. We introduce WISER-RL ({W}ake--sleep policy improvement loop, {I}mitation, and {S}elective {E}xperience {R}eplay), a composite reinforcement learning framework that turns assisted practice into autonomous control. During wake, GPTDAgger monitors disagreement among actions sampled by a diffusion policy. When disagreement crosses a threshold, a frozen GPT controller uses retrieved experience to continue the episode. During sleep, Conflict-Aware Experience Reweighting (CAER) compares visually matched successful trajectories and downweights conflicting action windows with more steps remaining to success. The policy imitates the reweighted successes and learns from both successes and failures through offline advantage-guided RL before collecting the next round. After final online PPO refinement, the autonomous policy succeeded in 100% evaluations on each of six LIBERO tasks and 100% trials on each of two real-robot tasks.

Introduction
A central goal of robotics is to acquire a new skill from one or a few human demonstrations and become proficient through practice
[
6

. A person can watch an example, reason about how it applies to a different scene, and gradually perform the skill with less deliberate effort. For robots, this motivates combining rapid adaptation from examples with lasting autonomous competence.
Reinforcement learning (RL) refines robotic policies through interaction
[

The challenge is to turn adaptation from a few examples into an autonomous policy that improves through practice.
WISER-RL couples fast episodic adaptation with slow policy consolidation (Fig.

A successful episode can contain a missed grasp and a recovery. When another episode reaches a visually similar state and grasps the object directly, both continuations receive the same terminal reward. Uniform imitation can therefore teach the retry alongside th

Conclusion
We introduce WISER-RL as a composite RL framework that couples fast episodic memory with slow policy consolidation through a recurring wake–sleep policy-improvement loop. Contextual assistance acquires experience, selective imitation consolidates successful behavior, and offline advantage-guided RL uses task outcomes to improve the policy that drives subsequent collection. GPTDAgger and CAER provide the experience-acquisition and replay-reweighting mechanisms within this composition. Online PPO further improves the policy through fresh autonomous interaction and achieve faster convergence to 100% success.
6
Limitation and Future Work
In simulation, WISER-RL uses a frozen VLM to guide action selection, allowing the wake–sleep loop to collect experience and improve the policy without human intervention after the initial demonstration. On the physical robot, operators still reset the workspace between episodes and intervene when hardware or control failures interrupt execution. Future work should evaluate whether dedicated reset and recovery policies can reduce both the number of robot interactions and the amount of operator assistance required to reach a fully autonomous policy consolidation.

Task and Evaluation.
For simulation tasks, we evaluate six LIBERO tasks: Goal-2, Goal-9, Spatial-5, Long-2, Long-5, and Long-8

The comparison baselines include RL100.
Implementation Details.

papers.title: Learning and Control in Physically Coupled Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Model Predictive Control via Proximal Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) enables real-time control of complex nonlinear systems but often incurs substantial computational costs due to repeated trajectory simulations. In this paper, we bridge policy optimization in reinforcement learning and sampling-based MPC to improve computational efficiency through sample reuse. Starting from a KL-regularized distributional formulation of trajectory optimization, we derive an exact performance-difference identity based on a signed exponential advantage function. This identity motivates two algorithms, PPO-MPPI and SPO-MPPI, which adapt proximal policy optimization techniques to sampling-based MPC, enabling multiple optimization updates using previously evaluated trajectories without additional forward simulations. We establish population-level monotonic improvement guarantees for both methods and prove convergence to first-order stationarity for PPO-MPPI under fixed-covariance Gaussian sampling distributions. Experiments on quadruped velocity tracking and quadrotor path tracking demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve competitive control performance at substantially lower computational cost than multi-stage sampling approaches. Our results establish a principled connection between policy optimization and sampling-based MPC and highlight the potential of trajectory reuse for sample-efficient predictive control.

papers.title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
papers.title_zh: LoRN：生成式机器人策略的低秩噪声引导
papers.abstract: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.

Abstract
Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights.
We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering.
However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models.
We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models.
A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample.
This separates the actor’s control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs.
Across three world-action models and ten model–task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering.
For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.
1
Introduction
Large robot foundation models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), can perform a wide range of behaviors.
For these models to reliably succeed on a particular task, they must learn to improve via interaction with their environment.
Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a way to improve their task performance through interaction, but updating large policies can be computationally expensive.
Noise steering has emerged as an approach to guide the denoising process of diffusion and flow-matching policies by replacing the initial noise samples.
However, these methods struggle to scale to high-dimensional noise inputs that are common in large policy classes such as VLAs and WAMs.
This work develops a noise steering method that addresses this challenge, focusing primarily on WAMs.
World-action models couple visual dynamics prediction with action generation.
Their sampling inputs include initial source distribution noise associated with both video and actions, and changing the video noise can also change the actions the model produces.
Existing action-noise steering methods do not exploit this input, and in the implementations and settings we evaluate they give no consistent improvement when applied to the substantially larger video-noise space.
In this work, we find that WAMs’ decoded actions are
more sensitive
to video noise than action noise, implying video noise may serve as a strong steering modality.
We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a method to efficiently train noise steering policies for world-action models.
Recent work has found that selecting the initial noise samples of diffusion or flow matching heads can effectively steer robot policies in a sample efficient manner without requiring any updates to the full model
[
26
]
.
We find that extending noise steering to large robot foundation models often fails, primarily because their noise inputs are high-dimensional and their sensitivity to it differs sharply between the video and action inputs.
LoRN overcomes these challenges by steering a low-rank projection of the noise distribution.
A steering actor outputs a low-dimensional vector that a fixed random projection lifts to the full noise dimension, which is then rescaled to resemble a Gaussian sample’s norm.
The frozen policy denoises this noise, and the actor is trained with reinforcement learning.
This formulation scales to high-dimensional action spaces and, most surprisingly, enables the steerability of the
video
noise to improve denoised actions.
Two design choices underlie our approach.
First, the actor controls only a small, low-rank subspace of the noise regardless of the input dimension.
We show that such a low-rank subspace contains directions that improve on the base policy with high probability.

Limitations
Noise steering relies on behaviors that the frozen policy can already produce.
Video noise provides a potentially expressive way to access these behaviors, but greater action variation does not necessarily translate into greater task success.
The sensitivity probe (

Learning useful control over this variation still requires interaction, and steering cannot directly teach the frozen model a missing skill.
Our analysis shows why a low-rank subspace can contain noise inputs that improve the policy, but does not establish how easily the actor can discover them.
The rank and training required for effective steering therefore remain empirical choices.
Similarly, preserving the native expected energy is a design choice, not a guarantee of the optimal noise scale for every policy: the identity holds for a fresh Gaussian sample independent of the actor’s output, which the fixed-draw DreamZero configurations do not satisfy (

Conclusion
We introduced LoRN, a method for improving frozen generative robot policies by steering their initial noise through a low-rank subspace.
A small actor controls the noise through a fixed random projection, while normalization and Gaussian mixing allow strong steering at a stable noise scale.
This enables steering of high-dimensional video noise in world-action models, giving the actor access to an input that can substantially influence the generated actions.
Across three world-action models and ten model–task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy

, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering.
The same approach supports action-noise steering across several policy families and transfers from simulation to a physical robot without hardware training.
Together, these results establish low-rank noise steering as a practical way to control high-dimensional generative robot policies, including through video noise that provides an expressive input for shaping their actions.

papers.abstract: When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video-action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning.   We find that the way video predictive training is supervised affects subsequent action learning. In our experiments, adapting at many noise levels yields a large gain, while adapting only at the noise level used at deployment yields none. Weight-transfer experiments further show that the gain stays with the adapted weights when they remain in the video generation model and disappears when they are used only to initialize the action policy. Initial loss and gradient measurements at the start of joint training indicate that target-domain predictive training gives the video model a better starting state, making subsequent joint learning of prediction and action easier. Under matched data and training budgets, predictive adaptation improves control. We evaluate the complete policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks.

Abstract
When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video–action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning.
We find that the way video predictive training is supervised affects subsequent action learning. In our experiments, adapting at many noise levels yields a large gain, while adapting only at the noise level used at deployment yields none. Weight-transfer experiments further show that the gain stays with the adapted weights when they remain in the video generation model and disappears when they are used only to initialize the action policy. Initial loss and gradient measurements at the start of joint training indicate that target-domain predictive training gives the video model a better starting state, making subsequent joint learning of prediction and action easier. Under matched data and training budgets, predictive adaptation improves control. We evaluate the complete policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks.

Introduction
When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already adjust their grip force in anticipation of upcoming load changes while their hand still deviates from the target path
[
1
]
. Prediction can develop well before skilled control. This motor-learning result suggests a question for video-driven robot learning: what training does the knowledge acquired by a video generation model need before an action policy can use it effectively?
Video generation models learn from large-scale visual data how scenes and objects change over time. Robot learning seeks to use this knowledge to help a policy generate actions from observations and task instructions. Existing methods train video prediction and action generation jointly

. Predicting how images change and learning the actions needed to complete a task, however, have different training objectives. A lower video-prediction error, on its own, says little about how well an action policy can use what the model has learned. We therefore ask two questions: how should a video generation model be further trained so that it provides more useful information for action learning, and which part of the model does the resulting gain come from?
We present ZERITH V2.5 (

The video generation model computes intermediate features from the current observation; the action policy reads these features and combines them with the task instruction, the robot state, and geometric information about the current scene to generate actions. Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Directions
10.1
Conclusion
This report asked what training a video generation model needs before an action policy can use its predictive priors effectively, with the demonstrations and the total number of updates held fixed. Across controlled comparisons, two conditions matter: how predictive training is supervised, and which module receives the adapted weights. ZERITH V2.5 summarizes the resulting recipe as
adapt the visual world, then scale the action policy
. Under a matched 30,000-update budget on the same demonstrations, devoting the first 3,000 updates to video-model-only adaptation improves LIBERO-Plus success by 17.55–19.16 percentage points across three geometric-conditioning variants with three seeds each, compared with 0.68–2.29 points from changing the operator within the same factorial study. The advantage also extends beyond a single endpoint. At matched Stage 2 update counts after the first few thousand updates, the policy built on the adapted video generation model leads direct training by 8 to 10 points at every recorded checkpoint; on the total-update axis, the staged schedule at 30,000 updates remains 18.18 points ahead of direct training at 50,000 updates.
Ablations and initialization probes show where this gain comes from and what it depends on. Crossing the two initialization sources shows that the benefit moves specifically with the adapted video-model weights: transferring them to the video generation model alone adds 19.67 points on LIBERO-Plus, whereas copying adapted layers into the action policy alone lowers success by 3.94 points. Scope.

Budget crossover.
On LIBERO-Plus, staged training trails direct training at 5,000 total updates and leads at every evaluated budget from 30,000 updates onward. The crossing lies between these budgets, but the evaluated checkpoints cannot pin it down. The staged 8,000-update checkpoint exceeds the direct 10,000-update checkpoint by only 0.14 points, and direct training was not evaluated at 8,000 updates. Placing the crossover in the 5,000–8,000-update interval therefore assumes that the direct score at 8,000 updates does not exceed its 10,000-update score. The broader 5,000–13,000-update interval (

Mechanism.
The initialization probes describe only the state at the start of Stage 2. The claim that this state makes action updates more effective remains a hypothesis; testing it would require an intervention. The analyses in

papers.title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.title_zh: RePlan-VLA：面向长程视觉-语言-动作模型的进度感知重规划
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

Abstract
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations.
Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework.
To this end, we introduce
RePlan-VLA
, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA’s short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution.
RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot’s motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes.
We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning.
Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of
$21.9\%$
and
$10.4\%$
in success rate over the next strongest baseline.
We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

Introduction
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models
[
27
,
29
,
11
,
23
,
15
,
8
]
have made significant progress toward developing generalist robotic policies capable of performing diverse manipulation tasks.
Despite their performance on short-horizon tasks (e.g. ‘Pick up the straw and place it in the cup.’), these models often struggle with reliable execution of long-horizon instructions (e.g. “Open the drawer, pick up the straw, navigate to the cup, and place the straw in the cup”).
This can be attributed to their inability to coordinate simultaneous progress tracking and execution of the long-horizon tasks, allowing small errors to propagate and cause downstream failures.
Towards this end, we propose decoupling of long-horizon reasoning, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery from a single-VLA policy to a VLA-agnostic framework, retaining the VLA policy only as a reliable executor of short-horizon tasks.

RePlan-VLA: Execution-aware replanning for long-horizon robotic manipulation.
Given a long-horizon language instruction and scene observations, RePlan-VLA decomposes the task into executable short-horizon subtasks, monitors the robot’s progress and detects discrepancies between intended and observed outcomes.
In this real-world rollout, the robot initially fails to place the white block into the bowl.
RePlan-VLA identifies the incomplete manipulation and replans to retry the failed subtask before proceeding with the remaining objectives.

Conclusion and Future Work
We present RePlan-VLA, a VLA-agnostic framework that improves long-horizon manipulation through visual progress estimation, failure-aware feedback, and adaptive replanning while preserving the capabilities of pretrained VLA policies.
Although its effectiveness depends on reliable visual grounding and the underlying policy’s short-horizon manipulation capabilities, and recovery may be limited by irreversible execution failures, RePlan-VLA provides a flexible approach to execution-aware long-horizon planning without modifying the underlying VLA.
Future work will explore skill-aware replanning that accounts for policy capabilities, learning from successful recoveries, and incorporating tactile sensing and other complementary modalities to improve progress estimation.

Object Search
Sausar Karaf

Abstract
Object search in unknown environments requires robots to gather useful observations while avoiding obstacles and accounting for limited sensor visibility. We present SearchDiffusion, a diffusion-based planner that generates position and heading trajectories using a learned dense utility map. The map represents geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress. It conditions trajectory generation and provides an objective for sampling guidance. Sampled map hypotheses provide additional geometric context, while geometric and heading guidance, validity checks, and analytical selection support execution. Across 90 simulated tasks on 24 map layouts, SearchDiffusion achieved 95.6% target detection at greater computational cost. Ablations show complementary benefits from utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime map hypotheses. In ten physical quadruped trials using OneMap relevance maps, eight were successful under operator assessment, without fine-tuning on real-robot data. These results support combining learned spatial utility with guided trajectory generation for object search under partial observability.
I
INTRODUCTION
Autonomous object search requires robots to gather useful observations while avoiding obstacles. Observation quality depends on the camera’s field of view, range, and viewing direction. Informative path planning therefore considers expected observation value alongside motion and safety constraints.
Diffusion planners learn trajectory distributions and generate candidates through iterative denoising
[
1
,
2
]
. Object search requires adaptation to new geometric and semantic evidence. Semantic relevance alone does not indicate accessibility or routes that provide useful views, motivating a spatial utility map that relates available evidence to search progress.
We propose
SearchDiffusion
, a trajectory planner that learns dense utility from geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic relevance. The predicted map conditions trajectory denoising and provides a differentiable objective for sampling guidance.

Counterfactual map hypotheses provide context about unobserved geometry while preserving observed free and occupied cells. Utility, geometric, and heading guidance refine candidates before validity checks and analytical ranking. The robot executes an initial portion of the selected trajectory, updates observations, and replans.
We compare detection, trajectory efficiency, and planning time under matched simulated conditions. Ablations disable inference components with network weights fixed. Physical robot experiments use OneMap

The main
contributions
are:
•
Utility-conditioned trajectory generation.
A learned dense utility map encodes geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress to condition trajectory diffusion.
•
Guidance, validation, and selection.
Utility, geometric, and heading objectives refine candidates during sampling. Validity checks and analytical scoring select a trajectory for partial execution.
•
Evaluation of component interactions.
Across 90 simulated tasks in 24 map clusters, SearchDiffusion improves detection over the tested baselines. Ablations support combining utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime hypotheses.
II
RELATED WORK
Classical exploration methods plan from the robot’s current map. Yamauchi
[
4

[
5

plans through known and unknown space while maintaining a stopping backup in known free space. EGO-Planner
[
6
]
derives obstacle-av

CONCLUSIONS
SearchDiffusion combines learned dense utility with diffusion planning for object search under partial observability. The utility map conditions trajectory generation and guides refinement, followed by validity checks and analytical selection. In matched simulations, the method achieved higher detection success across planning budgets than the tested frontier baselines, at greater computational cost. Deployment on a quadruped achieved an operator-assessed success rate of 80% without fine-tuning on real-robot data.
Ablations indicate complementary benefits: guidance reduced invalid-trajectory failures, while utility reduced failures caused by exhausting the search budget. Runtime map hypotheses provided limited additional detection benefit; removing them reduced computation while maintaining similar observed success. These findings support combining learned search utility with guided trajectory generation.
Future work will improve onboard planning efficiency, incorporate the robot’s physical footprint and sensing uncertainty into trajectory generation, and evaluate performance in a broader range of simulated and real environments.

EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
V-A
Experimental Setup and Evaluation Protocol
We evaluated 90 tasks across 24 maps using one inference seed, with matched initial poses, observed areas, targets, and sensing conditions. The simulated sensor had an 18-cell range, a
$60^{\circ}$
field of view, and obstacle occlusion. Runs allowed 200 planning cycles, executing up to ten poses per cycle. SearchDiffusion generated 32 candidates with ten denoising steps per decision.
Targets started undiscovered; runs ended at first detection. Success curves retain failures in the denominator and use planning cycles or travelled distance as budgets. Success–cycle AUC averages success over cycle budgets 1–200. Planning latency included map prediction, generation, guidance, safety checks, and selection, measured on 32 shared initial states on one workstation (RTX 4080

for learned models).
Excluding 51 tasks overlapping MapEx’s fine-tuning validation maps leaves 39 tasks across nine maps with no detected fine-tuning overlap.
We report 95% percentile confidence intervals from 2,000 map-cluster bootstrap resamples, drawing maps with replacement and retaining all their tasks. Shared resamples preserve paired method comparisons and ablation contrasts. Intervals do not capture inference-seed variability and are unadjusted for multiple comparisons.

Abstract
Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology–state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision–language–action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.

Introduction
Generalist robot policies learn from demonstrations across platforms
[
14
,
13
,
11
]
, but the kinematic meaning of joint-space actions depends on robot morphology. Identical joint values can produce different link poses as link lengths and joint arrangements vary; padding actions to a common dimension does not resolve this ambiguity. End-effector (EE) control provides Cartesian targets but requires robot-specific inverse kinematics and does not uniquely specify the full joint configuration. A shared joint-action representation should therefore preserve control coordinates while accounting for their morphology-dependent spatial effects.
To learn this relationship without collecting manipulation demonstrations for every morphology, we use robot kinematics as supervision. We introduce
MorphGen
, a procedural generator informed by a survey of 33 URDF/MJCF descriptions. MorphGen normalizes serial-arm kinematics into a common local-
$Z$
convention, samples six- and seven-joint manipulators from empirical link-length priors, and selects feasible home poses through collision-aware inverse kinematics. Forward kinematics provides link-pose targets for 40 million morphology–state pairs.
We present
RoboMorpher
, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer pretrained on these data. Morphology conditions its encoder and decoder, while kinematic-chain attention biases encode relative joint positions along the chain. Joint-angle reconstruction preserves control coordinates, and link-pose reconstruction supervises their kinematic effects. The pretrained tokenizer is then frozen and integrated into a vision–language–action (VLA) policy. Following Discrete Forcing
[
21
]
, a discrete branch predicts action codes, which are decoded into coarse trajectories and refined by a continuous flow-matching branch. Pretrained morphology features condition both branches.
We evaluate on 15 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks across five embodiments
[
3
]
and introduce
EmbodiBench
, comprising ten tabletop tasks with 30 generated URDFs each. Downstream URDFs are excluded from tokenizer pretraining; policies learn from task demonstrations. RoboMorpher achieves 56.40% and 23.27% success, exceeding contin

Limitations
Unseen-URDF reconstruction does not establish zero-shot policy transfer: downstream policy training and evaluation lack a disjoint-morphology split. Survey coverage is limited, stacking remains difficult, and reconstruction has large outliers. Scaling behavior and variability across training seeds remain unmeasured (
Sec.
E.3
).
6
Conclusion
RoboMorpher learns morphology-conditioned action codes from MorphGen kinematic supervision and improves mean joint-space policy success on RoboTwin 2.0 and EmbodiBench. These findings support kinematic pretraining followed by task-specific policy learning. Ablations support link-pose supervision, particularly for lifting, while reconstruction exposes substantial outliers despite low average errors on unseen tokenizer URDFs. Improving stacking, reducing reconstruction tails, and testing policy transfer under disjoint morphology splits are important directions for future work.

papers.title: Phoenix: Learning Scene Structure Representations for Generalizable World-Action Models
papers.title_zh: Phoenix：学习场景结构表示以实现可泛化的世界-动作模型
papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling.
Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3’s general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge.

Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization.
Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation.

Conclusion
We presented Phoenix, which learns scene representations for generalizable world–action modeling. Phoenix Encoder builds on DINOv3’s visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents for joint prediction with appearance and actions. Representation learning uses approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data. After benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves SOTA performance on six simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning perturbation robustness, dexterous manipulation, and adaptation across robot configurations. Ablations validate both scene feature learning and generative compression. Phoenix also gains more from scaling pretraining data than a video-VAE-only baseline and adapts effectively with few downstream demonstrations. Better future-video prediction complements these policy results. Together, these findings connect scene representation learning with manipulation generalization and pretraining data efficiency.

papers.title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.
