Abstract
Robot learning systems require synchronized, high-quality demonstrations that combine visual, proprioceptive, and action data. However, collecting such datasets with mobile manipulators is often slowed down by fragmented teleoperation interfaces and manual post-processing workflows. This paper presents an integrated framework for teleoperated multimodal data collection on a Clearpath Dingo-O mobile base equipped with a Kinova Gen3 Lite manipulator and an Intel RealSense RGB-D camera. The framework combines single-controller operation of the base, arm, and recording process with an automated ROS-based pipeline for data capture, image-quality filtering, temporal synchronization, visualization, and export to machine-learning-ready Zarr datasets. We validate the system on a pick-and-place mobile-manipulation task in which the robot transports a bottle between two surfaces. The results show that the unified controller supports complete task execution and recording without external commands, while the data pipeline produces synchronized datasets for short demonstrations and identifies corrupted visual frames. The proposed framework provides a practical basis for producing structured demonstrations for robot-learning research. Code and videos of the experiments can be found at this
repo
.

Introduction
Mobile manipulators, such as the one in Fig.
1
, combine a mobile base with a robotic arm to interact with objects across large and dynamic workspaces. Achieving reliable autonomy remains difficult because the robot must coordinate many degrees of freedom in partially known or unstructured environments. Deep learning offers a promising path toward learning such perception and control behaviors from data

The experiments successfully validated the main functionality of the proposed teleoperation and data-collection framework. Four users without previous training were able to complete the pick-and-place task and record demonstrations without encountering major difficulties. This indicates that the controller mapping and recording procedure can be used by new operators with limited preparation. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the experimental evaluation was limited and should not be interpreted as a formal usability assessment. Its purpose was to verify that the integrated system operated correctly and that multiple users could collect demonstrations. A larger user study measuring task-completion time, error rates, learning effort, and operator workload is therefore left for future work.
The selected experiment imposed relatively modest requirements on the platform. It did not involve high-speed motion, precise object placement, or rapid coordination between the mobile base and manipulator. Consequently, the reliability of the framework under high-speed or high-precision operating conditions has not been established. Additional cameras and sensing modalities can also be incorporated in future versions of the framework.
Alternative input devices, such as a SpaceMouse and virtual-reality motion controllers, were also considered because they can provide more direct control over higher-dimensional motion. The DualShock 4 controller was selected because of

Conclusion
This paper presented an integrated framework for teleoperated multimodal data collection with a Dingo-O mobile base, Kinova Gen3 Lite manipulator, and end-effector-mounted RealSense RGB-D camera. The system combines single-controller operation of the base, arm, and recording process with an automated ROS-based pipeline for recording, image-quality filtering, temporal synchronization, visualization, and export to Zarr. In a mobile pick-and-place experiment, the unified controller enabled a single operator to execute and record complete demonstrations without external commands, while the data pipeline produced synchronized outputs for short-duration trials and rejected visually corrupted frames.
The experiments also revealed practical limitations that must be addressed before scaling to longer recordings or larger datasets. A natural next step is to run the full pipeline onboard the robot after adding dedicated solid-state storage, transferring only the final Zarr and cleaned rosbag files after processing. Future work should also include large-scale user studies that assess the framework and incorporate user feedback in the recording and operation process.

The robot used for this project consists of two separate parts. First is the base of the robot, which is a Clearpath Dingo-O

Only the final Zarr dataset and cleaned rosbag would then need to be transferred to the host laptop. Overall, the current experiments validate the feasibility of the integrated workflow, while broader usability studies and more demanding manipulation tasks remain necessary to evaluate its performance more comprehensively.

papers.title: Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking: Memory-Guided Adaptive Reasoning for Embodied Navigation
papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

papers.abstract: Robotic planning from visual observations and signal temporal logic (STL) requires grounding task requirements in scene evidence while adapting plans to execution feedback. We present GraF-VTA, a graph-based framework that extends Vision-TL-Action with structured task representations, causal observation history, and closed-loop trajectory generation. Bidirectional cross-attention fuses STL syntax tokens with visual features, while an optional frozen automaton embedding supplies complementary untimed task structure. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations and compresses older frames to provide recent execution context. Conditioned on these features and robot state, a flow-matching model generates plans whose action prefixes are executed before replanning from refreshed observations. Abstract
Robotic planning from visual observations and signal temporal logic (STL) requires grounding task requirements in scene evidence while adapting plans to execution feedback. We present GraF-VTA, a graph-based framework that extends Vision-TL-Action with structured task representations, causal observation history, and closed-loop trajectory generation. Bidirectional cross-attention fuses STL syntax tokens with visual features, while an optional frozen automaton embedding supplies complementary untimed task structure. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations and compresses older frames to provide recent execution context. Conditioned on these features and robot state, a flow-matching model generates plans whose action prefixes are executed before replanning from refreshed observations. Across five simulation environments, the single-graph configuration achieves higher open-loop Success@
$K$
than TeLoGraF and Vision-TL-Action on four environments at the reported budgets
$K\geq 16$
. On Panda, matched-update ablations increase Success@256 from 53.91% without observation history to 62.50% with pyramid memory. In closed-loop Dubins evaluation, it reaches 64.06% Success@1024, compared with 12.50% for adapted S-MSP and 27.34% for adapted Logic-VLA. These results support combining structured visual conditioning with observation history and replanning to improve coverage of STL-satisfying trajectories.

Introduction
Robotic tasks often combine goal achievement with deadlines, ordering, and obstacle avoidance. Signal temporal logic (STL) expresses these requirements precisely through spatial predicates and bounded temporal operators
[

]

Visual input provides a practical interface between STL planning and robot sensing, with grounding mechanisms relating symbolic references to image regions
[
18
,
24
,
30
]
.
Pretrained vision-language models have also been used to propose visual predicates and evaluate them from images, enabling the learning of symbolic world models for long-horizon planning
[
1
]
.
For STL-conditioned trajectory generation, TeLoGraF
[
35
]
conditions trajectory generation on syntax graphs containing exact object geometry, which must be supplied externally. End-to-end visuomotor learning
[
23
,
6
,
53
,
25
]
demonstrates that perception can instead be trained jointly with action prediction. Vision-TL-Action (VTA)
[
31
]
brings visual grounding to STL-conditioned generation by connecting logic nodes to image tokens. This supports a learned observation-to-trajectory mapping without exact object geometry in the STL specifications.
Executing trajectories planned by generative models is challenging because model mismatch, disturbances, and tracking errors can separate intended and realized motion. Receding-horizon STL control
[
39
,
38
,
33
]
and Diffusion Policy
[
7
]
motivate repeated planning from execution feedback. We therefore execute short action prefixes and refresh visual observations and robot state before generating subsequent actions, allowing plans to respond to observed deviations.
Refreshed observations alone may not reveal the robot’s recent interactions with the environment or the current task stage. MemoryVLA
[
40
]
demonstrates the value of historical perceptual and semantic information for temporally dependent manipulation. This motivates conditioning STL planning on causal observation history. A temporal pyramid preserves detailed current observations while compressing older frames, providing recent execution context within a finite memory window.
A complementary challenge is exposing task semantics to the generator. An STL syntax graph preserves composition, time bounds, and object references. Yet, as Xie et al.
[
46
]
observe for finite-trace LTL, equivalent formulas can have different syntax trees, complicating seman

Conclusion and Limitations
We presented GraF-VTA, which extends Vision-TL-Action with structured graph encoding, causal visual history, and action-prefix replanning for STL-conditioned trajectory generation. A temporal pyramid retains current visual detail and compresses past observations, while an optional frozen automaton embedding provides complementary untimed task structure. The single-graph configuration improves open-loop success coverage over the compared baselines in four of five simulated environments. Matched-update Panda ablations support the value of observation history, and Dubins comparisons demonstrate higher closed-loop coverage than adapted S-MSP and Logic-VLA.
Our evaluation uses simulated environments and semantic visual inputs, with gains varying across environments and no improvement on AntMaze. Success@
$K$
measures candidate coverage rather than reliable online selection or guaranteed STL satisfaction. Finite observation history and a static automaton embedding do not provide complete task-progress monitoring. The dual-graph extension remains insufficiently evaluated, and the pyramid’s additional gain over standard memory is modest. Future work will prioritize controlled component studies, replication across training seeds, and validation under real-world sensing and execution.

papers.abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $γ$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.

Abstract
Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback.
Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience.
We introduce
$\gamma$
-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence.
Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world.
BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents’ choice of valid solutions.
An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback.
Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience.
The resulting tool traces and aligned observation–action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation.
We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision.
Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.

Introduction
Recent advances in embodied agents have broadened how robot behavior is constructed and adapted.
Agents generate executable programs over perception and control interfaces
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Fu et al., 2026
)
, use execution feedback to revise programs and retain reusable skills
(
Lu et al., 2026
;
Huang et al., 2026b
)
, and combine learned action skills with analytic motion tools
(
Zhang et al., 2026e
)
.
Mobile agents use multimodal observations and action interfaces to pursue goals across multiple locations
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
In mobile manipulation, each action changes the conditions for the next.
Opening a cabinet changes access, grasping occupies a hand, and transport changes the conditions for placement.
To retrieve supplies from storage and deliver them elsewhere, an agent must coordinate these interactions and respond to their measured outcomes.
Existing activity benchmarks and generative environments provide valuable tasks and demonstration resources
(
Li et al., 2023
;
Dai et al., 2026
;
Nasiriany et al., 2026
)
.
We ask how a physical world can support complete-task evaluation while retaining the interaction context needed to construct and revise behavior.
We introduce
$\bm{\gamma}$
-Scape
, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for complete mobile manipulation tasks (
figure

).
The platform combines
370 indoor scenes
with
11,073 interactive object assets
for task construction.
Task agents compose their own programs and tool calls, combining motion tools and learned skills according to the states reached during execution.
BenchForge
turns structured task requirements into physical instances by binding resources, constructing connected layouts, and applying geometric and physical checks.
Each instance includes an instruction, a reference program, and a goal evaluator.
The reference program supports construction and collection, while the evaluator checks requested outcomes and process conditions.
This separation lets researchers compare agent-chosen solutions under a fixed task definition and retain the same goals when revising behavior.
Different embodiments and shared-space participants provide additional physical contexts for studying these behaviors.

Conclusion
We introduced
$\gamma$
-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence.
The platform connects grounded task construction, agent-directed execution, and reusable experience within persistent physical worlds.
BenchForge compiles task objectives into physical instances and explicit goal criteria.
Shared interfaces let agents compose programs, motion tools, and learned skills, with different solutions evaluated against the same task-goal criteria.
The benchmark results show that broad task-family coverage can coexist with low instance-level completion.
Carrying and coordination remain particularly challenging across the evaluated systems, while recorded episodes reveal how contact quality, reachability, and base stability affect subsequent actions.
Complete-task success and accumulated semantic progress distinguish satisfaction of task conditions from intermediate accomplishments, supporting analysis of both completed tasks and partial execution.
The collection studies connect local contact outcomes with subsequent transport and placement, and show how a retained failure record can inform an executable program revision.
Tool traces support program refinement, while aligned observation–action records from agentic, assisted, and human-guided execution provide material for skill adaptation.
Together, these capabilities connect behavior construction with experience reuse under common task goals.
They provide infrastructure for studying repeated adaptation and embodied recursive self-improvement.

steps.text:
1) 输入结构化目标，由BenchForge落实为含指令、参考程序与评估器的物理任务实例。
2) 智能体在持久物理世界中组合运动工具与学习技能，执行导航与操作。
3) 收集接触交互、工具轨迹及对齐的观测–动作记录。
4) 以统一任务目标标准进行后续评估。
